entities.name: Adrian I
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Pope Adrian I (reigned 772–795) had the longest pontificate of the eighth century and one of the most consequential in the entire first millennium. His reign coincided with the rise of Charlemagne, and the partnership he forged with the Frankish king transformed the political and religious landscape of Western Europe. Adrian I requested Charlemagne's military intervention against the Lombards in 773–774, resulting in their defeat and the establishment of the Papal States as an independent political entity — the foundation of papal temporal sovereignty that would endure until 1870.

Adrian I's reign saw the consolidation of the Donation of Constantine's ideological use — the claim that Emperor Constantine had granted the papacy temporal sovereignty over Italy — and the practical establishment of a papal territorial state protected by Frankish military power. His close relationship with Charlemagne, expressed in a famous correspondence, shaped the model of Church-state relations that would dominate medieval European thought for centuries.

At the Second Council of Nicaea (787) — the last ecumenical council recognised by both East and West — Adrian I's legates played a key role in the restoration of icon veneration after the first phase of Byzantine Iconoclasm. His pontificate thus touched the central theological controversy of the Byzantine world while simultaneously reshaping the political geography of the Latin West. His death in 795 was mourned by Charlemagne with an inscription that survives to this day.
